name: Fatima Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to your employer, AI companies, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. What is a normal day on your crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Fatima Schmidt, 43, and I joined an electricity company line crew after getting my vocational certificate. I’m the junior one, so I lay out barriers, prepare tools and follow the senior worker through each isolation check before we touch a line. I like tracing a fault from the customer calls to the actual damaged fitting. I still misjudge how long a repair will take when a pole looks fine from the ground.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the workday look like at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ben leaves early for the bakery, so I handle breakfast for our two school-age children unless I have a callout. We have a mortgage, but my shift premiums put me high on the lineworker pay scale and we have more than six months saved. There are plenty of other utilities nearby. I use AI every day to turn my field notes into quizzes and to compare my rough travel estimates, but a senior person checks every safety decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a bit of faster paperwork is useful, even if the grand claims fizzle. A system that finds the right old work order saves us a search in a van full of folders. I’d still ask someone who was on the job what really happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be pleased because I get more time to learn faults without a sudden change in the job itself. I am not yet the worker who sees a cracked insulator from across the street. Our savings and good shift pay let me take that learning seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep using my AI quiz after dinner and add a photo-free description of each fault I’ve seen. In the first year I’d ask the senior worker to check those descriptions once a week, then keep taking normal repair shifts. I would not buy new equipment for a small office saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little amused at all the noise for a quicker folder search. I can learn with a stable crew. The weather and my own mistakes still deserve respect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you remember a fault you described wrongly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wrote down a fault as a loose connector last month; the senior worker showed me the heat mark that made it a damaged joint. The correction went straight into my quiz that evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the household plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben and I would leave the emergency account and mortgage transfer alone. The children’s school costs are ordinary bills we have already planned for.

say: I would welcome **faster work orders** without claiming the physical repair has changed.
I would still ask a **crew member** what happened on an older job.
think: I need more **fault experience**, and a stable crew gives me room to learn.
Our **savings and shift pay** make the small technology change easy to absorb.
do: Add each new **fault description** to my AI practice quiz after dinner.
Ask the senior worker for a **weekly check** and keep normal repair shifts.
feel: Calm and slightly amused by the **grand claims** around a modest paperwork saving.
S0.quote: A system that finds the right old work order saves us a search in a van full of folders.
fieldNote: Fatima already uses **daily AI quizzes** and turns a senior worker’s correction about a damaged joint into practice.
She welcomes a **shorter records search** while remaining frank about her junior skill and the continuing physical repair.

steps.text: Add new fault descriptions to the AI quiz after dinner
Keep taking normal line repair shifts with weekly senior checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues the planning desk will change before our climbing work does. I’d volunteer to test the new route planner with a real week of callouts, especially the jobs where a gate key or road closure delays us. If its numbers are wrong, I want that written down before anyone sets a quota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may lose people, and the crew may get less help finding parts. My physical job looks safe for now, but a squeezed route could cost us overtime, which is part of my higher pay. I like a useful tool, but I cannot feed my children with a clever timetable that cuts the paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the dispatcher for a copy of our old routes, then run the proposed planner beside them for a month. I’d show the supervisor differences in travel time and missing stock, and keep my normal line shifts. During the first year I’d learn how to correct job locations in the software, so bad data does not follow the next crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a chance to stop wasteful driving, and I can also see our day being squeezed. The savings make a short pay dip manageable, but I do not want a permanent one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the route trial log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d mark the job that sends us back to the depot for a fuse we should have carried. A route that is ten minutes shorter on a screen can leave a street dark an extra hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at home if overtime falls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben and I could cover the mortgage on base pay. If overtime shrank for several months, we’d put the planned kitchen repaint off until we saw a reliable new rota.

say: I would test the **route planner** on actual callouts before management sets targets.
I would record gate delays and **stock gaps** that a tidy route misses.
think: Our physical repair work remains, but **overtime** could fall as office staffing and routes change.
Our **base pay** covers the mortgage, although a lasting shift cut would matter.
do: Compare **old and proposed routes** for a month with the dispatcher.
Learn to **correct job locations** in the software while keeping paid line shifts.
Delay the **kitchen repaint** if overtime stays lower for several months.
feel: Uneasy about lasting **paid-hour cuts**, despite seeing a chance to reduce wasted travel.
S1.quote: I cannot feed my children with a clever timetable that cuts the paid hours.
fieldNote: Her enthusiasm for software is bounded by **paid hours**; she links route targets directly to the household budget.
She proposes a **side-by-side route trial** with stock and access notes, a specific test before changing crew expectations.

steps.text: Compare route software with a month of actual callouts
Keep taking paid line shifts during the route trial
Delay the kitchen repaint if overtime stays lower

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the thinking system comes in 2028 and the capable repair robots around 2031. Those are three years apart, and I expect to be climbing and fixing lines between them. I’d ask the company to let workers test any robot on awkward jobs before it changes the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 I could still earn on the truck while reports and planning become cheap. At 48, if robots handle damaged conductors as well as people, being the eager junior tech user will not guarantee my post. I have a reserve and nearby utilities, but I could lose the shift premiums that make this mortgage easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask for a funded place in network fault analysis and check whether the company has real posts for graduates. I’d keep taking line shifts in 2028 and 2029 while learning the approved diagnostic screen. If robots reduce my crew in 2031, I’d apply for fault-analysis vacancies here and at nearby utilities, and pause our large holiday while the pay settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can move quickly, but the calendar still moves faster than an apprenticeship. I feel more worried about a post disappearing than about learning the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the course coordinator for the number of funded seats and past graduates who actually got paid jobs. I do not want a certificate that looks good on a wall while the field roster shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children that my work may look different, but I am still working and applying. Ben and I would review the mortgage only after we knew the new wage, not frighten them with a guess.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AI** from repair robots arriving around 2031.
I would ask for **worker trials** on awkward field jobs before the roster changes.
think: I expect **paid linework** during the gap, but robot repairs could remove my junior post later.
Our **reserve and local jobs** buy options without protecting the current shift premiums.
do: Request **funded fault-analysis training** and check graduate job numbers now.
Keep paid **line shifts** through 2029 while learning the approved diagnostic screen.
Apply for **analysis vacancies** and pause the large holiday if crews shrink in 2031.
feel: Anxious about a **vanishing post**, even though I am comfortable learning the new equipment.
S2.quote: I do not want a certificate that looks good on a wall while the field roster shrinks.
fieldNote: Fatima does not treat technology fluency as **job protection** once capable robots can do physical line repairs.
Her quick response includes **funded training and applications**, with a course judged by actual paid placements.

steps.text: Request funded network fault-analysis training this month
Keep taking paid line shifts through 2029
Apply for fault-analysis vacancies if 2031 crews shrink
Pause the large holiday while new pay settles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the electricity company to publish a test schedule for field robots and let lineworkers report failures without being blamed. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, but the hands-on machines come around 2034. A real test log from winter repairs would tell us more than a product video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when thinking AI arrives, I should be far more useful on a crew than I am now. By 51, when robots arrive, I might have a route into testing or fault diagnosis if there are paid posts. I cannot assume my knack for tools means I get one. The children will be older, but we will still have a mortgage and need income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the maintenance manager whether lineworkers can join a supervised robot trial. I’d keep doing paid repairs and collect fault cases I can explain without customer details. In 2032 I’d apply for a posted diagnostic role if the wage is close to my shift pay; in 2034 I’d compare outside utility offers if the robots cut field hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the extra time is useful. I can build field judgment while testing the new equipment. I would feel cheated if the company used our trial notes and then left us off the hiring list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fault would you put in the robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a machine can recognise a cracked clamp hidden behind wet tape. I have missed a fault from the ground myself, so the trial needs to include cases that fool humans too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a diagnostic offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben and I would calculate the daytime diagnostic wage against shift premiums. A steadier evening at home would help, but the mortgage still needs a number, not a feeling.

say: I would seek a **winter test log** and worker reporting before 2034 field robots arrive.
I would distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from later machine repair work.
think: I may have stronger **field judgment** by 2031, yet a paid diagnostic post is not promised.
The older children reduce some care needs, but our **mortgage and wage** still matter.
do: Ask the manager about a **supervised robot trial** and keep paid repairs.
Prepare **fault cases** without customer details for the test team.
Apply for a **posted diagnostic role** in 2032 if its pay works.
feel: Uneasy but engaged, with enough **time to test** equipment and seek a real post.
S3.quote: A real test log from winter repairs would tell us more than a product video.
fieldNote: Her proposed **winter trial** draws on actual line faults, including cases that can fool experienced workers.
She weighs a diagnostic post against **shift premiums**, making her technology interest conditional on household income.

steps.text: Keep taking paid field repair shifts during the trial
Join a supervised robot trial if the manager allows it
Apply for a posted diagnostic role in 2032 if pay works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues we have time to ask for yearly figures, not just a single promise. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, when I’m 53, and capable field robots around 2039, when I’m 56. I’d want the company to publish how many repair and diagnostic posts remain as it tests machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then our children will be grown, and Ben and I may want less shift work. I could picture moving to daytime fault review, but I do not know what our retirement income will be. A strong savings balance is useful; it is not permission to assume I can stop earning at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request a retirement estimate and compare it with our mortgage schedule. I’d keep paid linework going while taking funded diagnostics training when the company offers a place tied to a real vacancy. In 2037 I’d apply for a daytime fault-review post if one opens; in 2039 I’d decide on fewer callouts only after seeing the pay and retirement figures together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. I have enough time to learn the trade well and test a second route. I’d grow uneasy later if the promised post counts never appeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which retirement figures would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask payroll for a monthly retirement amount after deductions. We can change our schedule when the children are adults, but I won’t count their earnings as part of our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a yearly post report show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want the company’s report to separate crew jobs from diagnostic jobs, and filled posts from advertisements. A list of vacancies nobody fills would make the future look rosier than it is.

say: I would request **yearly post counts** for repair and diagnostic work.
I would mark **2036 thinking AI** and 2039 field robots as separate decisions.
think: Our children will be **grown**, but I cannot assume retirement income replaces my wage at 56.
A **daytime fault role** could suit us if it pays enough to carry the mortgage.
do: Request a **retirement estimate** and compare it with the mortgage now.
Continue paid **linework** while seeking funded diagnostics training tied to vacancies.
Apply for a **daytime fault-review post** in 2037 if one opens.
feel: Calm with a decade to prepare, though missing **post counts** would unsettle me later.
S4.quote: A strong savings balance is useful; it is not permission to assume I can stop earning at 56.
fieldNote: Her long view tests **retirement income** and job counts rather than treating savings as a lifetime wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the repair robots follow before I have much field experience. Give us paid training tied to posted jobs and let crews test machines on real storm damage. I would also want the yearly staffing numbers where everyone can see them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn’t ask who owns a wrong fault prediction when the street is dark. I would keep a human name beside every machine recommendation. Someone has to answer the telephone when the map is wrong.

headlineQuote: Someone has to answer the telephone when the map is wrong.
portrait: Fatima is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with vocational training, high shift pay, a mortgage and two school-age children.
She uses **AI daily** for fault quizzes, yet has senior workers verify safety choices she has not mastered.
Strong savings and **local utilities** offer options, though the household depends on shift premiums and continued paid work.
She seeks **field trials and diagnostics**, judging every course and post by real vacancies and wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable repair robots could arrive before she has gained much field experience.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid training** tied to vacancies, worker tests on storm damage and published staffing numbers.
